name: Sonnō jōi
summary: Sonnō jōi, 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians', was the late-Tokugawa nationalist slogan and programme that grew out of the Mito school. It held that Japan's ruling line descends from the sun goddess, that loyalty to the emperor is the basis of morality (the kokutai), and that the Western powers were barbarians to be kept out, whatever arms Japan borrowed from them. In the 1850s and 1860s its followers turned it against a shogunate that had signed the treaties, and it was abandoned after the Restoration.

scope: The late-Tokugawa (Bakumatsu) slogan and programme as the defining sources present it: Aizawa Seishisai's 1825 Shinron and the kokutai doctrine, the Mito school's imperial loyalism and anti-foreignism, and the loyalists around Kyoto, Mito and Chōshū who used the slogan against the treaties and the shogunate. It excludes the later emperor-system nationalism of the Meiji state, which took over parts of Aizawa's programme but dropped the expulsion of foreigners.

notes: The record is thin: no full text of the Shinron or of Yoshida Shōin's writings was available, and the defining sources are short. Themes searched without finding a position: economy, taxation, welfare, civil liberties, family and gender, courts, elections and federalism, technology, ecology and international organisations. The slogan itself was never a worked-out programme on these; the Meiji state replaced it with fukoku kyōhei. Aizawa himself rejected the use of the slogan against the shogunate (s2), while the loyalists acted on it (s5); the revolution answer follows the record.
